```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 5.5,
  fig.height = 3.5,
  fig.align = "center"
)
options(digits = 4)
```

*discoverHTE* estimates what a continuous exposure does on average, and then asks
whether it does the same thing to everyone. The exposure-response function (ERF)
describes how the expected outcome changes as the exposure moves across its range with
the measured covariates held fixed, and `estimate_erf()` estimates it. `rpart_erf()`
then searches a set of candidate effect modifiers for subgroups whose ERFs differ,
returning a tree whose nodes each carry their own dose-response curve.

Estimating the curve and partitioning on it are separate steps on purpose. The ERF is estimated once, with whatever nuisance
models suit the data, and the tree is then grown from that fit without re-estimating
anything. This vignette walks through both, using the `nhanes3lead` dataset from
*adrftools*: blood lead level and a mathematics test score for 2,521 children.

```{r}
library(discoverHTE)

data("nhanes3lead", package = "adrftools")

head(nhanes3lead[c("Math", "logBLL", "Age", "Male", "PIR", "Race")])
```

The exposure is `logBLL`, the log of blood lead level in µg/dL, and the outcome is
`Math`. The remaining variables are the covariates we will adjust for.

# Estimating an exposure-response function

`estimate_erf()` takes a two-part formula: the outcome on the left, then the exposure and
the covariates separated by a `|`. Everything to the right of the `|` is adjusted for.

```{r}
erf <- estimate_erf(Math ~ logBLL | Age + Male + PIR + Smoke_in_Home + Race,
                    data = nhanes3lead)

erf
```

The estimator is the doubly robust one of @kennedyNonparametricMethodsDoubly2017. It
forms a pseudo-outcome from two nuisance functionals, the conditional mean of the outcome
and the conditional density of the exposure, and then smooths that pseudo-outcome against
the exposure with a local linear regression. Being doubly robust means the ERF is
consistent when either nuisance model is correct, not only when both are.

The most useful part of the returned `<erf>` object is its `erf` component, a function
that evaluates the curve wherever we ask and returns the estimates with their covariance.

```{r}
est <- erf$erf(c(0, 1, 2, 3))

est$est

sqrt(diag(est$vcov))
```

Lead is associated with a lower score throughout: moving from a log blood lead level of 0
to 3 is associated with a drop of about
`r round(diff(range(erf$erf(c(0, 3), vcov = FALSE)$est)), 1)` points on a test whose
scores run from 0 to 20.

## The bandwidth

The local linear regression needs a bandwidth, and selecting it by leave-one-out
cross-validation is usually the slowest part of a call. The bandwidth that was used is
stored on the object.

```{r}
erf$bw
```

Passing a number to `bw` skips the search, and passing a function applies it as a rule of
thumb. When we only want to re-smooth an ERF we have already fit, `update()` does that
without fitting the nuisance models again, which is much faster than a fresh call.

```{r}
erf_smooth <- update(erf, bw = 2 * erf$bw)

erf_smooth$bw
```

# Displaying the ERF

Plotting an `<erf>` draws the curve, a confidence band, and the distribution of the
exposure along the top.

```{r}
plot(erf)
```

The band is simultaneous by default, meaning it covers the whole curve at the stated
level rather than each point separately. A simultaneous band is the one to read when
making a claim about the shape of the curve, since a pointwise band understates how much
of the curve could be consistent with the data. Pointwise bands are available with
`simultaneous = FALSE`, and `conf_level = 0` omits the band entirely.

```{r}
plot(erf, simultaneous = FALSE, density = FALSE)
```

The result is a `<ggplot>` object, so it takes the usual *ggplot2* additions.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

plot(erf, density = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Blood lead and mathematics score",
       x = "log blood lead level", y = "Expected score")
```

# Choosing how the nuisances are estimated

The `method` argument decides how the two nuisance functionals are estimated, and is
where most of the modeling judgment goes. Each `method_*()` function returns an
`<erf_method>` object that `estimate_erf()` then calls.

`method_glm()`, the default, fits generalized linear models: a linear model for the
exposure, and for the outcome a linear model with a natural cubic spline on the exposure.
It is fast and a reasonable starting point, but it commits to a parametric form for both
nuisances.

`method_superlearner()` stacks several learners and chooses the combination with the best
cross-validated prediction error, which avoids committing to one form. Because the
stacking is cross-validated, a seed is needed for replicability.

```{r eval = rlang::is_installed("SuperLearner")}
set.seed(1234)

erf_sl <- estimate_erf(Math ~ logBLL | Age + Male + PIR + Smoke_in_Home + Race,
                       data = nhanes3lead,
                       method = method_superlearner(
                         SL.library = c("SL.mean", "SL.glm", "SL.rpart")))

erf_sl
```

`method_gamlss()` models the whole conditional distribution of each variable rather than
only its mean, which matters when the exposure density is skewed. `method_bartisan()`
uses Bayesian additive regression trees, and reads the exposure density directly off the
fitted response distribution rather than recovering it from standardized residuals.
`method_negbinomcens()` handles count outcomes measured over several observations per
unit with interval-censored cells, and is the subject of
`vignette("negbinomcens")`.

Arguments reach the underlying models through `outcome` and `exposure`. One point is
worth care: `exposure` defaults to `outcome`, so a family chosen for the outcome is
handed to the exposure model as well unless we say otherwise.

```{r}
nhanes3lead$Math_count <- round(nhanes3lead$Math)

erf_pois <- estimate_erf(Math_count ~ logBLL | Age + Male + PIR + Race,
                         data = nhanes3lead,
                         method = method_glm(outcome = list(family = poisson()),
                                             exposure = list(family = gaussian())))

erf_pois
```

# Inference

Several arguments control how the standard errors are formed.

`crossfit` splits the sample into folds, fits the nuisance models on all but one fold and
evaluates them on the one held out, then rotates. This removes the bias that comes from
using the same observations to fit the nuisance models and to evaluate them, which is
what makes the influence-function standard errors trustworthy when flexible learners are
used.

`cluster` names a clustering variable, and puts it to two uses: it computes a
cluster-robust variance, and it forms the cross-fitting folds over whole clusters so that
no observation's nuisance prediction is trained on its own cluster-mates. Only one
clustering variable is allowed, because the folds need a single partition of the sample
to follow.

```{r}
erf_cf <- estimate_erf(Math ~ logBLL | Age + Male + PIR + Smoke_in_Home + Race,
                       data = nhanes3lead, crossfit = 5)

sqrt(diag(erf_cf$erf(1, vcov = TRUE)$vcov))
```

`trim` caps the ratio of the marginal to the conditional exposure density when the
pseudo-outcome is formed. Where the conditional density is very small the ratio can be
enormous and a handful of units come to dominate the fit, so the default of `0.99` caps
it at its 99th percentile. Setting `trim = 1` disables it.

Sampling weights are supplied through `weights`, either as a vector or as the name of a
column in `data`. `nhanes3lead` carries the NHANES examination weight.

```{r}
erf_wt <- estimate_erf(Math ~ logBLL | Age + Male + PIR + Smoke_in_Home + Race,
                       data = nhanes3lead, weights = "MEC_wt")

erf_wt$erf(1, vcov = FALSE)$est
```

## The derivative of the ERF

Sometimes the quantity of interest is not the curve but its slope: how much the expected
outcome changes per unit of exposure at each point. Setting `d = 1` estimates that
derivative directly, with standard errors on the same scale.

```{r}
erf_slope <- estimate_erf(Math ~ logBLL | Age + Male + PIR + Smoke_in_Home + Race,
                          data = nhanes3lead, d = 1)

plot(erf_slope, density = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(y = "Change in expected score per unit of log blood lead")
```

A derivative is harder to estimate than the curve itself, so the band is wide. Where it
covers zero, the data are consistent with the ERF being flat at that exposure. The degree
of the local polynomial follows `d`, and the bandwidth is selected for that degree, so an
ERF and its derivative do not generally share a bandwidth.

# Partitioning the sample

`rpart_erf()` takes a fitted `<erf>` and a one-sided formula naming the candidate effect
modifiers, and splits the sample recursively. At each node it searches every candidate
split and keeps the one whose two subgroup ERFs differ most.

```{r}
tr <- rpart_erf(erf, ~ Male + Race + PIR + Smoke_in_Home,
                max_depth = 3, min_samples = 100)

tr
```

The measure of "differ most" is the `metric` argument. `"L2"`, the default, integrates
the squared difference between the two branch ERFs over the exposure range; `"L1"` uses
the absolute difference, `"AUC"` the difference in areas under the two curves, and
`"fANOVA"` each branch's squared deviation from the parent. `"AUC"` responds to a
difference in level, while `"L2"` and `"L1"` also respond to a difference in shape, so
two curves that cross can score high on `"L2"` and near zero on `"AUC"`.

`int_weight_method` decides where over the exposure range those differences count. Both
`"density"` and `"gps"` weight by the product of the two branches' exposure densities,
which concentrates the objective where both subgroups actually have exposure mass and
keeps a split from being rewarded for extrapolating into a region only one subgroup
occupies. `"none"` weights the range uniformly, which gives the exposure tails more say
and so tends to surface differences in slope.

A continuous modifier has to be cut into candidate groups before it can be split on, and
two arguments control that. `cont_var_splits` sets how many groups, and `split_type` sets
where the cuts fall: `"quantile"`, the default, puts roughly the same number of units in
each group, while `"range"` spaces the cuts evenly on the scale of the modifier. The two
differ once a modifier is skewed, where even spacing can leave a group holding very few
units. A unit missing the modifier a split is made on goes to the right branch, and the
candidate cut points are read off the observed values alone.

# Reading the tree

`summary()` draws the tree. Each node is numbered, labeled with the split it descends
from, and annotated with its size; a leaf is marked with `*`.

```{r}
summary(tr)
```

The numbers come from a depth-first walk that counts every node, leaves included, and
they are the positions everything else uses. `tree[[i]]` extracts the ERF at node `i` as
a thin `<erf>` that can be plotted on its own.

```{r}
tr[[2]]
```

```{r}
plot(tr[[2]], density = FALSE)
```

The subtitle is the node's branch path, so a node ERF lifted out of its tree still says
which subgroup it describes.

Plotting the tree itself draws a panel at every internal node, each showing the ERFs of
that node's two children, positioned according to the shape of the tree.

```{r fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
plot(tr)
```

`type` sets the shape of the output: `"tree"` for the single plot above, or `"list"`
for the panels separately, named by the node numbers `summary()` shows. `panels` sets
what each panel contains: `"children"` for one curve per child, as the tree above draws,
or `"marginal"` for the node's own single ERF, which gives every node a panel including
the leaves.

```{r}
panels <- plot(tr, type = "list")

names(panels)

panels[["1"]]
```

A marginal panel shows the same curve that `plot(tr[[i]])` draws, so the two views are
consistent with one another.

# Honest trees

The ERF itself is a confirmatory estimate: cross-fit, with influence-function standard
errors, and cluster-robust where clustering is supplied. A tree grown and evaluated on
the same data is not. It searches many candidate splits and keeps the best, so the
subgroup bands at its nodes do not pay for that search and are narrower than honest bands
would be. The split points in particular are unstable; a modifier that appears high in
the tree is more trustworthy than the exact threshold it was split at.

`honest_erf_tree()` separates the search from the estimation. It splits the sample in
two, estimates an ERF on each half, grows the tree on one of them, and then estimates the
ERF at every node of that tree on the other, which played no part in choosing the splits.
Given the tree, the bands at its nodes then have the same standing as the band of an ERF
estimated on a subgroup fixed in advance. The arguments are those of `estimate_erf()` and
`rpart_erf()` together, plus `frac`, the fraction of the sample used for discovery.

```{r}
set.seed(1234)

ht <- honest_erf_tree(Math ~ logBLL | Age + Male + PIR + Smoke_in_Home + Race,
                      data = nhanes3lead,
                      modifiers = ~ Male + Race + PIR + Smoke_in_Home,
                      max_depth = 3, min_samples = 100)

ht
```

The result is an `<erf_tree>` whose node sizes and node ERFs come from the inference
half, so `summary()`, `[[`, and `plot()` read it as before. The tree the search found on
the discovery half is kept as its `discovery` component, and each internal node carries
the value of the split objective on both samples.

```{r}
summary(ht)

c(discovery = ht$tree$metric_discovery, inference = ht$tree$metric)
```

The objective is smaller on the inference sample, which is the search's optimism made
visible: the split was chosen because its estimated difference was the largest among the
candidates, and an independent sample gives an estimate of the same difference free of
that selection. The two phases can be run separately with `split_sample()`,
`estimate_erf()`, `rpart_erf()`, and `refit_erf_tree()`, which is useful when the
discovery tree should be inspected before anything is estimated on the inference sample;
`vignette("negbinomcens")` does so.

The price is sample size: each half has less power than the whole, so an honest tree
finds fewer splits and draws wider bands than the same tree grown on everything. Treat an
unsplit tree as a way of generating hypotheses about who is most affected, and an honest
one as the way to estimate the curves of the subgroups it proposes.
